newsitem.title: USA: Police mount huge manhunt for Versace killer.
newsitem.headline: Police mount huge manhunt for Versace killer.

text.p: Police and FBI agents scoured south Florida on Wednesday in "an intense manhunt" for the alleged serial killer and homosexual prostitute accused of murdering Italian fashion king Gianni Versace.
Police said tips and leads were flooding in from the public on the possible whereabouts of Andrew Cunanan, one of America's most wanted men even before the Versace slaying.

"There are leads from all over ... some of them appear to be fruitful and some don't," Jim Chambliss, chief of investigations at the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, told a news conference. "It's a very large manhunt, it's an intense manhunt."
FBI Special Agent in Charge Paul Philip said Cunanan could still be hiding in the Miami region, though police did not rule out that he could have fled.
"We're going to concentrate our search right here," Philip said. "He might not be able to (flee) ... It's quite possible he might be holed up some place."
Cunanan was wanted in connection with four previous murders, including that of his former male lover, during a two-week, cross-country killing spree that began in Minneapolis in April.

Police were using old-fashioned shoe leather and high-tech computer networking to distribute flyers with photographs of Cunanan. The FBI internet website showing its 10 Most Wanted suspects included a $10,000 reward for his capture but had not yet been updated to mention the Versace slaying.

Maureen Orth, a writer working with Vanity Fair magazine, told NBC television on Wednesday that friends of Cunanan said he had met Versace once backstage at the San Francisco opera and that the designer appeared to recognise him.
Police said they did not know if Versace, a homosexual, had any relationship with Cunanan.
Versace, who dressed the world's most beautiful people, was shot twice in the head on the steps of his Miami Beach mansion by a gunman on Tuesday morning.
Chambliss told Reuters that police had not recovered the murder weapon.
Versace's sister Donatella, a respected designer in her own right, visited her brother's mansion and later left in a limousine, witnesses said.

Miami Beach Police Chief Richard Barreto said Cunanan, who had been spotted in the Miami area as long as two weeks ago, "was laying in wait for him ... it appears to me that this was a planned event ... an execution-type incident."
Arthur Furia, president of the Italy-America Chamber of Commerce, said a Mass would be held in honour of Versace on Friday in Miami Beach and would be open to the public.
Residents of Miami Beach, usually a pulsating playground for models, fun-seekers and tourists, did not wait to pay their respects though.
Groups of sombre onlookers kept vigil outside the wrought-iron gates of Versace's luxury Mediterranean-style mansion on Ocean Drive.
They built a shrine of flowers and candles on the steps where he had slumped dead, blood pouring from two head wounds, after the killer struck.
Shock and disbelief reverberated from the cafes and model agencies of Miami Beach, an area he had helped revitalise, to the capitals of the fashion world over which he reigned.

Versace, 50, symbolised Italian fashion to the world and dressed the likes of Princess Diana, singers Madonna, Sting and Elton John, and actresses Demi Moore and Liz Hurley. He had built a multimillion-dollar empire after learning the basics of fashion from his mother.
He was killed as he walked home after buying magazines at the News Cafe on Ocean Drive, a beach-front street of renovated art deco hotels and trendy restaurants.

The killer ran away and several hours later police named Cunanan as the sole suspect. Barreto said a red truck found by police in Miami after the killing belonged to Cunanan's last alleged victim, a New Jersey cemetery caretaker shot dead in May.
Police said Cunanan was armed and dangerous and warned gays and lesbians in particular to be on guard.
"It appears that on occasion he frequents places where gay folks hang out," Philip said. But he added: "Nobody's safe in this. Everybody's at risk. Everybody's got to help us put this guy in jail."
